reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

analysis.body:
Measured adoption in this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For finance and insurance, NAICS 52, the latest figure is 41.0%, against 36.5% in the prior period, with the question first asked in September 2023. That is the broadest official number in this material, and it covers finance and insurance as a whole rather than banks alone, so it is not a bank-only adoption rate.

This site's own coverage describes fraud detection and credit models as decades old in banking, with generative AI in service and compliance as the new frontier, all of it under Federal Reserve model risk supervision. Evident Insights, whose Evident AI Index is described here as the benchmark, benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services and says banks are among the businesses racing to incorporate the technology into almost everything they do, and that several of the world's biggest banks have quietly become AI-powered behemoths. The index scores major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics covering talent, innovation, leadership and transparency, and Evident has extended the format regionally, with an index for banks in Latin America, an inaugural index for banks in the Middle East and Africa, and a separate index for insurance whose 2026 results it covers.

On the vendor and model side the material is thinner. This site's Financial Models page catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub with licence, downloads and release date, refreshed daily from the Hub's public API and sorted by all-time downloads. Evident positions itself as the intelligence platform for AI in financial services and publishes a Banking Brief with over 15,000 subscribers across banking, tech, consulting, academia and government, which shows where benchmarking attention concentrates rather than where deployment money goes.

The sources give almost no quantified return on investment for banking AI. Evident's insurance index material refers to where the technology is starting to unlock value and where insurers should focus next, which is directional rather than a measured result, and nothing in these excerpts reports a cost saving, revenue gain or productivity figure for banks. A reader looking for hard ROI evidence will not find it here.

Regulatory posture is the clearest part of the picture. Credit and anti-money-laundering models operate under the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, and the letter is listed in the Fed's 2011 supervisory letters index, which makes banking the sector where AI governance predates the current AI boom by more than a decade. Two cited pages do not carry the AI content their labels suggest. The harvested Federal Reserve page text concerns guidance on prior notices for dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies, and the harvested Treasury page text concerns OFAC sanctions against 28 individuals and businesses in a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money laundering network under Executive Order 13818, plus background on International Anti-Corruption Day and the 189 parties to the United Nations Convention against Corruption. Neither excerpt states AI-specific findings, so the supervisory framing attributed to Treasury is not visible in the text captured here.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the practical reading is that adoption is already mainstream at the sector level per the Census Bureau, that the public scoreboard to compare against is Evident's index and its talent, innovation, leadership and transparency metrics, and that any model touching credit or anti-money-laundering lands inside a model risk management regime in force since 2011. The open-model catalogue on this site is a starting point for build versus buy questions, not a deployment guide. Where these sources are silent, on bank-level adoption rates, on measured returns, and on AI-specific supervisory guidance in the Treasury excerpt, the honest answer is that the material does not say.

https://evidentinsights.com/.brief: Evident Insights is an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across the financial services sector. It supplies data, research, and benchmarking to help financial services leaders make informed AI-related decisions, investments, and strategic choices. The platform publishes the Evident AI Index, which ranks banks and insurers on their AI deployment and highlights emerging trends. Since launching in January 2023, the index has sparked debate and received widespread press coverage, with Evident CEO Alexandra Mousavizadeh frequently commenting on global AI trends.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The site catalogues what it calls the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, giving each model's licence, download count and release date, with the list refreshed daily. It states that the entries are drawn from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, and that every model links to its own Hub page. The page records a last-verified date of 2026-09-27.
